pages.title: [Adobe Stock Strategy] Is it dangerous to create tags at the same time as prompts? How to automatically generate "49 tags that perfectly match the image" using MidStock's image analysis｜​マサヒコ｜個人開発 × AI・ストック攻略
pages.text:
[Adobe Stock Strategy] Is it dangerous to create tags at the same time as prompts? How to automatically generate "49 tags that perfectly match the image" using MidStock's image analysis
When generating images for Adobe Stock with Midjourney, do you ask AI like ChatGPT to "create the title and tags for submission at the same time as the prompt!"?
While this method may seem efficient at first glance, it actually has a major pitfall in the stock photo industry.
That is the problem that the content instructed in the prompt and the actual content of the image output by Midjourney do not necessarily match.
In this article, I will explain, along with actual screens, why the "feature to generate a title and 49 tags from a completed image" included in the iOS/Android app 'MidStock' that I developed is directly linked to improving the review pass rate and the number of downloads.
■ The discrepancy that occurs when you "create prompts and metadata at the same time"
When using Midjourney, it is common for elements written in the prompt to be omitted, or conversely, for small items not specified to be drawn.
For example, suppose you created 49 tags at the same time when creating the prompt, assuming a "dinner with a wine glass, bread, and vegetables."
However, what if the best image that actually came out of Midjourney did not have a wine glass or bread, but instead had a "candle" and a "wooden spoon" drawn in them?
If you use the tags from when you created the prompt as they are, the following negative effects will occur.
・Tags that do not exist in the image (wine, bread) are mixed in, leading to Adobe Stock review rejections or lower evaluations in search algorithms
・Attractive elements actually drawn (candles, wooden spoons, specific types of vegetables) are missing from the tags, so they do not show up in buyer searches
In other words, to create accurate metadata that actually sells, you need to "show the finished image directly to the AI and reverse-engineer the tags from what is depicted," rather than "creating tags from the prompt."
■ Demonstration: Creating "perfectly matching metadata" from a single finished image
Now, I will show you how accurately metadata can be created from a generated image using the "Image Analysis" feature of "MidStock."
The image we will analyze this time is this illustration of a warm dining table.
On the plate are three types of roasted vegetables, next to it is wooden cutlery, in the back are a candle and a cup, and slightly visible in the background, rather than the foreground, is a person's clothing.
▼ Step 1: Select the finished image in the "Image Analysis" tab
Open the "Image Analysis" tab at the bottom of the app, select the image saved on your smartphone, and tap "Analyze one image at once" (multiple images can also be selected and analyzed in bulk).
Tapping will start the AI visual analysis.
▼ Step 2: Title and category completed by reading every corner of the image
Once the analysis is complete, the created metadata is saved in the "Library" tab.
・Japanese Title: Plate of roasted vegetable dishes lined up on a dining table lit by candles
・English Title: Plate of Roasted Vegetables on Dining Table with Candlelight
Not only is the main subject of roasted vegetables accurately reflected in the title, but the situation of the "dining table lit by candles" is as well.
▼ Step 3: 49 tags that perfectly match the ingredients and accessories depicted
Scroll down the screen further to see the 49 automatically generated tag keywords.
・English tags (top excerpts): #roasted vegetables #dinner table #beetroot #carrot #potato #food #candle #plate #cutlery #dining #tablecloth #vegetarian #healthy #meal #wooden spoon ...
・Japanese tags (in order of priority, 49 items): Roasted vegetables, dining table, beetroot, carrot, potato, food, candle, plate, cutlery, dinner, tablecloth, vegetarian, healthy, meal, wooden spoon, fork, napkin, cup, pottery, candlestick, flame, candle...
This is the most important point to note.
Because the AI is looking directly at the actual image, it doesn't just settle for calling the vegetables on the plate 'vegetables,' but accurately identifies them one by one as 'beetroot,' 'carrot,' and 'potato.'
Furthermore, the 49 tags are filled with elements actually present in the image, including the 'wooden spoon,' 'fork,' and 'napkin' placed on the right, the 'pottery cup' and 'candlestick/candle' in the background, and even keywords for the atmosphere and seasonal feel like 'autumn/winter' and 'cozy.'
▼ Step 4: Supports art style determination and 'fine-tuning by looking at the image'
If you scroll further to the bottom, you will also be automatically guided through settings that are often confusing when submitting to Adobe Stock.
・Content created with generative AI tools: Yes
・Identifiable people or property: No (People: No, Property: No)
Since this image was not a photograph but had an anime/illustration-style touch, the AI detected the art style and automatically determined the file format as 'Illustration.' It also accurately judged that the person in the background, whose face is not identifiable because only part of their clothing is visible, means 'Identifiable people: No,' and guides you accordingly.
Even if you want to 'strengthen specific keywords a little more,' you can easily brush them up at any time using the 'Fine-tune by looking at the image' or 'Re-analyze' buttons at the bottom.
■ Straight to submission with CSV export and SFTP transfer
Once the accurate title and 49 tags are complete, you can proceed directly to the submission process using the 'Export / SFTP Transfer' button on the bottom right.
・Light Plan (300 yen/month): Unlimited prompt generation & metadata generation from images
・Standard Plan (680 yen/month): In addition to the above, supports CSV bulk export & 'SFTP transfer' to upload images directly to Adobe Stock from the app
・Premium Plan (1,100 yen/month): Supports direct metadata embedding into image files & vector (SVG) conversion
※Note: To use the AI features of this app, you need to set your own AI API key (such as Google's Gemini API or OpenAI API). By using your own API key, the API cost remains around a few dozen yen even if you analyze hundreds of images (you can also utilize free tiers), and the app itself is offered at an affordable price starting from 300 yen per month.

Please experience the 'satisfaction of 100% matching images and tags' and the comfort of finishing submission work in just a few seconds on your smartphone.

pages.text:

Developer Uses Claude AI to Build 7 Free Adobe Alternatives
A developer used Claude AI to recreate seven Adobe apps for free. See how ArtCraft works, its limitations, and what it means for software development.
A developer used AI to create free, open-source alternatives to Adobe Creative Cloud applications, including Photoshop, Illustrator, and Premiere Pro. Image: Screengrab from ArtCraft
We may earn from vendors via affiliate links or
sponsorships. This might affect product placement on our
site, but not the content of our reviews. See our Terms of Use for
details.
Adobe’s subscription-based creative software has an unlikely new challenger: a collection of free applications built with the help of AI.
Developer Brandon Thomas has created ArtCraft, an open-source project that recreates the look and some functionality of popular Adobe applications, including Photoshop, Illustrator, and Premiere Pro. Using Anthropic’s Claude AI and the Rust programming language, Thomas has developed alternatives that users can access without Adobe’s subscription fees.
The project shows how AI-assisted coding can help individual developers tackle complex software projects. But early reviews suggest that recreating familiar interfaces is easier than matching the functionality of professional applications.
Seven AI-built apps recreate Adobe’s creative tools
ArtCraft’s initial releases include seven applications modeled after Adobe’s creative software.
According to AppleInsider, Thomas along with other vibe coders developed the applications using AI-assisted programming, in which developers use natural-language prompts to help generate and refine software. The project includes:
The applications and their source code are available through Thomas’s GitHub repositories.
Thomas describes the software as clean-room implementations, meaning the applications are intended to reproduce functionality without copying Adobe’s proprietary source code. That remains the developer’s characterization rather than an independently verified legal assessment.
The project targets macOS, Windows, and Linux, although compatibility and available features may vary by application.
How well do the free Adobe alternatives work?
ArtCraft’s most recognizable feature is its resemblance to Adobe’s interfaces.
AppleInsider tested PhotoCraft and found a familiar layout, including editing tools, icons, and a layers panel resembling Photoshop.
However, the similarities do not necessarily extend to the underlying functionality.
In separate testing, TechRadar reported problems with PhotoCraft’s HEIC image support and file-saving options. Its review also identified limitations in FilmCraft, including missing or incomplete video-editing functions.
These shortcomings matter for professionals who depend on reliable editing tools, consistent file handling, and compatibility with existing projects.
For now, the applications remain experimental, and independent testing has not established that they can replace Adobe’s software in demanding production workflows.
ArtCraft’s significance extends beyond the possibility of free creative software.
With Claude assisting in development, Thomas has built applications resembling products that typically require considerable programming effort.The project illustrates how AI coding assistants can help developers create interfaces, prototype features, and refine software without manually writing every component.
However, the limitations identified in early testing reveal an important distinction between building software quickly and making it dependable.
A convincing interface may be relatively straightforward to reproduce, but professional applications also require reliable file handling, accurate output, and consistent performance across different workflows.
That distinction matters for businesses evaluating AI-generated software. Development speed may reduce the effort needed to produce an initial application, but it does not eliminate the work required to test, secure, maintain, and support it.
ArtCraft offers a visible example of that trade-off. Its applications demonstrate the possibilities of AI-assisted development while showing why functional completeness remains a challenge.
SS&C Intralinks DealCentre AI vs. Datasite: Which platform is built for the future of dealmaking?
SS&C Intralinks FundCentre AI vs. Juniper Square: Which platform better supports modern private markets fund managers?
Why Data, Not Models, Determines AI Success
The Rise of the AI-Native Factory: How Physical AI Is Transforming Manufacturing
Could AI-built software challenge subscription tools?
ArtCraft also raises questions about how AI-assisted development could affect competition in the software market.
Thomas has cited frustration with Adobe’s subscription and cancellation practices as part of his motivation for creating free alternatives. By helping smaller developers build recognizable applications, AI coding tools could lower some of the barriers to entering markets dominated by established software providers.
However, competing with Adobe involves more than reproducing its interface or basic editing features.
Businesses rely on file compatibility, technical support, ongoing updates, and established workflows. These factors can make switching software costly even when an alternative is free.
Thomas has already extended his approach beyond Adobe, developing open-source applications inspired by Microsoft Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, according to Tom’s Hardware.
For IT leaders, the development highlights a potential shift in software purchasing decisions. As AI makes it easier to build alternatives, organizations may have more options, but they will still need to weigh cost savings against reliability, security, and long-term support.
ArtCraft may not be ready to replace Adobe Creative Cloud, but it raises a question for businesses: as AI makes software easier to build, what will make it worth paying for?

Adobe Inc. (ADBE) is Attracting Investor Attention: Here is What You Should Know
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 7:00 AM CDT 5 min read
Adobe Systems (ADBE) has recently been on Zacks.com's list of the most searched stocks. Therefore, you might want to consider some of the key factors that could influence the stock's performance in the near future.
Shares of this software maker have returned -1% over the past month versus the Zacks S&P 500 composite's +0.7% change. The Zacks Computer - Software industry, to which Adobe belongs, has gained 6.3% over this period. Now the key question is: Where could the stock be headed in the near term?
While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.
Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.
Our analysis is essentially based on how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to take the latest business trends into account. When earnings estimates for a company go up, the fair value for its stock goes up as well. And when a stock's fair value is higher than its current market price, investors tend to buy the stock, resulting in its price moving upward. Because of this, empirical studies indicate a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and short-term stock price movements.
For the current quarter, Adobe is expected to post earnings of $6.32 per share, indicating a change of +14.9% from the year-ago quarter. The Zacks Consensus Estimate remained unchanged over the last 30 days.
For the current fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $24.47 points to a change of +16.9% from the prior year. Over the last 30 days, this estimate has remained unchanged.
For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $27.7 indicates a change of +13.2% from what Adobe is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has remained unchanged.
Having a strong externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, offers a more conclusive picture of a stock's price direction in the near term, since it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. Due to the size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, Adobe is rated Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).
The chart below shows the evolution of the company's forward 12-month consensus EPS estimate:
12-month consensus EPS estimate for ADBE
While earnings growth is arguably the most superior indicator of a company's financial health, nothing happens as such if a business isn't able to grow its revenues. After all, it's nearly impossible for a company to increase its earnings for an extended period without increasing its revenues. So, it's important to know a company's potential revenue growth.
In the case of Adobe, the consensus sales estimate of $6.84 billion for the current quarter points to a year-over-year change of +10.4%. The $26.6 billion and $29.06 billion estimates for the current and next fiscal years indicate changes of +11.9% and +9.2%, respectively.
Last Reported Results and Surprise History
Adobe reported revenues of $6.76 billion in the last reported quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +12.9%. EPS of $6.13 for the same period compares with $5.31 a year ago.
Compared to the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $6.69 billion, the reported revenues represent a surprise of +1.02%. The EPS surprise was +0.82%.
The company beat consensus EPS estimates in each of the trailing four quarters. The company topped consensus revenue estimates each time over this period.
No investment decision can be efficient without considering a stock's valuation. Whether a stock's current price rightly reflects the intrinsic value of the underlying business and the company's growth prospects is an essential determinant of its future price performance.
While comparing the current values of a company's valuation multiples, such as price-to-earnings (P/E), price-to-sales (P/S), and price-to-cash flow (P/CF), with its own historical values helps determine whether its stock is fairly valued, overvalued, or undervalued, comparing the company relative to its peers on these parameters gives a good sense of the reasonability of the stock's price.
The Zacks Value Style Score (part of the Zacks Style Scores system), which pays close attention to both traditional and unconventional valuation metrics to grade stocks from A to F (an A is better than a B; a B is better than a C; and so on), is pretty helpful in identifying whether a stock is overvalued, rightly valued, or temporarily undervalued.
Adobe is graded B on this front, indicating that it is trading at a discount to its peers. Click here to see the values of some of the valuation metrics that have driven this grade.
The facts discussed here and much other information on Zacks.com might help determine whether or not it's worthwhile paying attention to the market buzz about Adobe. However, its Zacks Rank #3 does suggest that it may perform in line with the broader market in the near term.

pages.title: Wall Street Has Its Eyes on Adobe. Here's Where the Stock Could Be Headed. - 24/7 Wall St.
pages.text:
Wall Street Has Its Eyes on Adobe. Here’s Where the Stock Could Be Headed.
Adobe is down nearly 28% this year yet still beating earnings estimates and raising guidance, which raises an uncomfortable question about whether the market has gotten the AI disruption story completely wrong.
Published October 19, 2026, 8:00am ET · 3 min read
Price Targets desk. Editor: Vandita Jadeja.
Adobe is a multinational software company best known for its Photoshop and Acrobat. © Adobe logo (CC by 2.0) by midiman
The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE | ADBE Price Prediction) is $294.54 over the next 12 months. With shares trading at $252.88, that works out to 16.5% upside. The stock gets a buy rating with high confidence.
Price Target from 24/7 Wall St.
Adobe’s growth is holding up and guidance keeps rising, yet the stock is priced as if its business is shrinking. That gap drives the call. At a forward P/E of about 9x, the market has already priced in a lot of fear about AI disruption.
The open question is whether Adobe can turn rapid AI adoption into a clear acceleration in annual recurring revenue (ARR). We think the current price leaves enough room for that to work.
Shares gained 5.07% today and 8.64% over the past week. Shares remain down 4.79% over the past month and 27.75% year to date. The stock sits 30.5% below its 52-week high of $363.70 and 33% above its low of $190.12. The bounce came right after a widely read Barron’s report on a downgrade to Sell over growth concerns.
The latest results were solid. Fiscal Q3 revenue rose 12.9% to $6.76 billion, ahead of the $6.70 billion consensus. Non-GAAP EPS of $6.13 beat the $6.09 estimate. Management also raised full-year non-GAAP EPS guidance to $24.45 to $24.50. Leadership is changing too: Anil Chakravarthy becomes CEO on December 1, and Shantanu Narayen stays on as executive chair.
Adobe’s AI-first ARR now exceeds $650 million and is growing more than 150% a year. Firefly ARR rose 40% quarter over quarter. Creative freemium users passed 100 million, up more than 70%. Adobe has also held off on pricing actions to build its user base first, which gives it room to raise prices later.
Capital returns add support: Adobe bought back 9.5 million shares last quarter and has $24.55 billion left under its authorization. Of the analysts covering the stock, 11 rate it Buy or Strong Buy, and the consensus target is $272.31. The bull case is $326.20.
Remaining performance obligations grew just 8%, and analysts pressed management on net new ARR. Five analysts rate the stock Sell or Strong Sell. Net income rose only 3.1%.
On the other side of the ledger, free cash flow grew 14.68%, and much of the profit lag reflects planned investment in freemium growth. The bear case is at $254.03.
Adobe Trades at a Steep Discount to Microsoft and Salesforce
The benchmark for AI monetization at scale is Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT). It has more than 30 million paid Copilot seats and grew quarterly revenue 17.75% while trading at about 30x trailing earnings.
Adobe Experience Cloud faces direct competition from Salesforce (NYSE:CRM). It grew revenue a slower 10.83% yet trades at 26x trailing earnings.
Adobe is growing faster than Salesforce at a far lower multiple. Next to that peer group, our 24/7 Wall St. price target looks conservative.
What Could Make or Break Adobe From Here
The 24/7 Wall St. price target remains at $294.54, with a buy rating and 90% confidence. Valuation is the deciding factor.
Shares could outperform if AI-first ARR keeps growing at triple digits and the new CEO starts turning freemium users into paying ones. The bear case gains weight if net new ARR keeps slowing into fiscal 2027.
Price Target from 24/7 Wall St.
Adobe would need to keep executing on its current strategy for these projections to hold. Generative AI competitors could drive results well below this path, while faster monetization of its user base could drive them well above it.
Contact [email protected] for any questions or corrections.
Vandita Jadeja is a financial publisher with over a decade of experience writing about financial topics, including investment, savings, retirement, insurance and banking. Vandita is a Chartered Accountant who loves to debunk financial concepts for readers.
Her work has appeared on sites that include The Motley Fool, InvestorPlace, and Benzinga. She covers investing and focuses on stock picks and price prediction for 24/7 Wall St.
When not looking for the next stock investment opportunity, she can be found traveling, reading, chasing sunsets and enjoying her iced latte.

pages.title: An open-source Adobe suite built with AI is almost ready to replace the real thing
pages.text:
His love of PCs and their components was born out of trying to squeeze every ounce of performance out of the family computer. Tinkering with his own build at age 10 turned into building PCs for friends and family, fostering a passion that would ultimately take shape as a career path.
Besides being the first call for tech support for those close to him, Ty is a computer science student, with his focus being cloud computing and networking. He also competed in semi-pro Counter-Strike for 8 years, making him intimately familiar with everything to do with peripherals.
As someone who has worked within the Adobe suite for a long time, I'm almost constantly looking for alternatives, and that has nothing to do with the quality of the first-party apps themselves. They're excellent to work in and provide a professional workflow that I'm used to, but paying monthly for a piece of software has never sat right with me. I have consistently gone back and forth, canceling and renewing my subscription because the alternatives I find just don't cut it, but that cycle seems to have mercifully come to an end.
When developer Brandon Thomas released ArtCraft's "crafting apps," they immediately caught my attention. It’s a set of seven open-source apps modeled on Adobe’s flagship programs, built in Rust with Claude Opus 5.5. The UI is a spitting image, the feature parity is most of the way there for a weekend creative like me, and it's free with no subscription required. It has some rough edges and missing features, but for a project that's not even two months old, it's way better than it has any right to be.
The apps have virtually all of the same menus and workflows
I'm someone who is essentially totally self-taught on the Adobe platform, having started with Premiere Pro to edit sick gaming montages when I was quite young, and found Photoshop and Lightroom later. I'm not a professional, but I know my way around these apps well.
Upon first launch of FilmCraft, the Premiere Pro equivalent, it opens to a sample project with some clips and a pre-built sequence, but I was more interested in how it would handle 4K gameplay capture. I treated it exactly as I would Premiere, importing the footage, cutting it with all of the same keybinds I usually use in the Editing workspace, and it's 1:1 here.
This will be a theme, but it's incredibly impressive how well recreated some of the UI is. I moved on to adding some effects to the gameplay, starting with a "Damaged VHS" effect on one of the clips, and for a canned effect, it looks pretty good. I then tested some key-framing with a crop, and besides some of the colors in the UI being different, I can't tell the difference between this and Premiere. Exporting is the same, and most of the settings you'd expect to be there are present, complete with hardware acceleration.
PhotoCraft was the next thing I tested, and because Photoshop is what I use most for daily work, my expectations are quite high. Some of the work I do requires passing around .psd files, and being able to open those natively is a non-negotiable. PhotoCraft opens all of the templates I use for work instantly, and does so with zero fuss. Good start.
I moved into working with a standard template I use most frequently that consists of multiple layers, and everything is exactly where it should be. Adjustment layers, masks, layer styles, and type all exist. Actions are there too, though PhotoCraft doesn’t include Photoshop’s prebuilt set, so you record your own.
LightCraft is the Lightroom equivalent, and it's modeled on the cloud-based Lightroom rather than Lightroom Classic. Compared to the other Lightroom alternatives I've used like darktable and Affinity, LightCraft is already just as good for what I do, which is quick edits on photos that I want to use for publication. It can't use Adobe's servers for some of the AI features like denoising, but it does provide a way to upload your own model that runs locally on your own hardware. I haven't tested this myself, but if it works even half as well as the Adobe offering, I can see myself swapping over the LightCraft full-time.
It's far more usable than the usual Linux alternatives
I'm the first person that will go to bat for FOSS software, but if we're being honest with ourselves, stuff like GIMP and kdenlive is not a suitable replacement for the kind of workspace that Adobe offers. Professionals simply cannot choose Linux as their sole operating system if they rely on Adobe software, so they've historically been stuck dual-booting Windows or using a Mac. Dragging Adobe software kicking and screaming through Wine was not a fun experience personally, but I can acknowledge that good work is being done there.
Thankfully, though, I think ArtCraft is the first signal that we might not need to force the round peg through the square hole much longer.
Every ArtCraft app ships with a native Linux build, and that, to me, is the biggest selling point of all. Using these apps on Windows was great, but it's able to solve the OS exclusivity problem that creatives have had, and that's huge.
The ArtCraft project is pretty clear about its gaps, and some of them are going to be deal-breakers for those who use creative software for paid work. By its own count, PhotoCraft has 56 of Photoshop’s 68 tools. It’s slower than Photoshop at almost everything the team has timed, and it doesn’t support Photoshop plugins. Most importantly for anyone with clients, the PSDs it saves aren’t yet reliably accepted by Photoshop.
LightCraft’s own numbers tell a similar story. By feature count it claims about 81% of Lightroom. As a day-to-day replacement, the project puts it nearer 61% overall and around 51% for a typical working photographer. RAW handling is definitely the weak spot. The project says LightCraft can decode 83% of the 1,446 camera models Adobe supports, but has verified only 38% of them. It works best for JPEG and DNG shooters on one machine and for most Sony, Panasonic, Fujifilm, Nikon, and older Canon RAW files. Plug-in and ecosystem support sits around 15%. For my Canon EOS REBEL T3i, it imported everything just fine, but your mileage will certainly vary.
FilmCraft's roadmap is pretty similar, with its feature checklist covering 87% of Premiere, but the team's own estimate of readiness for real work is 50 to 60%. The theme is the same here: plugin support is the real gap for pros, being unable to work with VST3 or Audio Units plugins, and it doesn’t support third-party OpenFX video effects. Lumetri, keys, masks, and export rendering still run on the CPU as well, which isn't good for anyone doing professional work.
There’s also the question of whether ArtCraft will be around long enough to rely on. Thomas calls the apps clean-room reimplementations built from public specs and observed behavior, but having been built with Opus 5.5, some critics call that into question. There's also the issue of copying Adobe's interface this closely, raising some questions about trade dress, and while Adobe hasn't made any comment at the time of writing, they could have a case for breach of contract of their General Terms of Use at the very least, as it bars reverse engineering specifically.
For an alpha, the ArtCraft suite is incredibly impressive
If you're a professional that requires compatibility with a specific set of third-party plugins and hardware acceleration, I wouldn't cancel your Creative Cloud subscription just yet. If you’re a hobbyist or a working creative whose jobs mostly involve retouching, layout tweaks, editing some quick video or culling a shoot, ditching Adobe for these ArtCraft apps is probably safe. It costs nothing to download these apps and take them for a spin, and if it keeps progressing at this rate, the result might be the ultimate FOSS creative suite.

pages.title: Adobe Rebuilt Photoshop And Premiere For NVIDIA's RTX Spark Platform
pages.text:
Adobe rebuilt Photoshop and Premiere for NVIDIA's RTX Spark platform
The apps were optimized to work faster on RTX Spark computers.
Add Engadget on Google:
Adobe has "rearchitected" its creative apps, including Photoshop, its video editing software Premiere and its 3D design platform Substance 3D to "take full advantage" of NVIDIA's RTX Spark, according to company VP Deepa Subramaniam. RTX Spark is NVIDIA's new system-on-chip (SoC) that's meant to give Windows laptops and small desktops the capability to run AI tasks locally on device. Unlike NVIDIA's DGX Spark, which mainly targets companies and AI developers, RTX Spark is more accessible to creatives and novice developers.
"Our apps like Photoshop, Premiere and Substance are trusted by the world's most talented storytellers, from photographers and designers creating iconic campaigns, to filmmakers and editors bringing award-winning film and television to life, to artists creating characters and visual effects that bring those stories to the screen," Subramaniam said. "For this audience, performance across creative workflows is critical to allow them to stay focused on their story and craft."
Subramaniam said the optimized apps are two times faster when it comes to AI tasks and editing across workflows. The redesigned Photoshop will be more responsive and faster at rendering complex workflows on computers with RTX Spark. Users will be able to see the changes they make in real time, such as when they're applying effects like Light Leaks (example in the image above) or removing elements from images with the Remove tool.
Meanwhile, Premiere users will be able to enjoy "real, tangible speed gains" when it comes to rendering, applying effects, AI-powered editing and color-grading for audio and video. Finally, the optimized Substance 3D Painter "speeds up the heaviest steps around texturing," as well as many other tasks, such as opening and saving large projects and exporting textures.

pages.title: “Software is over”: Bold AI developer takes aim at Adobe with open source clones - Ars Technica
pages.text:
For a while, those hoping to avoid the difficulty and expense of dealing with Adobe’s Creative Suite have been able to use several free and/or open source alternatives that replicate some or all of those capabilities. Now, one developer is using AI-powered reverse engineering to mimic the look, feel, and functionality of Adobe’s well-known software with what he hopes will soon be perfect fidelity.
Artcraft got its start last year as a “controllable AI for artists” that allows for precise post-generation editing of AI-crafted images and videos. Over the weekend, though, the brand debuted its pivot to a suite of seven open source apps recreating the user interface and tools found in Adobe’s Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro.
In announcing those new apps on Reddit earlier this week, software developer Brandon Thomas said he used Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 to create “clean-room replacements” for Adobe’s closed source software in Rust (with WebAssembly versions available for use in a browser). And while commenters on Hacker News and elsewhere have taken pains to point out the new software’s many current shortcomings, Thomas makes the grandiose promise that the current “super early alpha” state will soon lead to something just as functional as anything Adobe has ever put out.
“We’re going to reach 100% [feature] parity within a month,” Thomas stated on Reddit of his plans to quickly squash bugs and add features with the help of community reports. Days later, on Hacker News, he amended that position slightly to say that “99% parity will take a while, but I’m sure it’ll be measured in months and not years.”
Is software over?
Thomas, who says he has about a decade of experience working on large-scale Rust projects, wrote on Hacker News that he was inspired to create his own open source Adobe software alternatives after being “bit by the dark pattern ‘cancellation fee’ one too many times.” Development of the totally free options offered here under MIT/Apache licenses will be funded, Thomas wrote, by selling token-based access to the pre-existing Artcraft visual AI model and IDE, which is offered as an imagery-generation option inside the apps alongside third-party models. This revenue stream will help ensure these apps aren’t “going to be some orphaned small-team project,” Thomas wrote. “We have a team building popular software for filmmakers, so supporting this is fully funded.”
Filmcraft closely mimics the look and feel of Adobe Premiere.
Credit:
Filmcraft closely mimics the look and feel of Adobe Premiere.
Credit:
Thomas is the latest in a long line of coders using AI tools to speed up the long-standing but labor-intensive practice of reverse engineering (i.e., replicating the functionality of a piece of software without directly copying the code itself). While that practice has generally been found legally acceptable, the ArtCraft apps could still face legal trouble if their “trade dress” too closely mimics Adobe’s familiar appearance and interface.
After coding exclusively with AI tools since February, Thomas said he foresees a near future when everyday developers can re-create open source versions of popular paid software to “take back the internet and own tech forever.”
“Now you can just create 1:1 functional equivalents, clean room, that are highly performant and cross-platform. Nothing is stopping you,” Thomas wrote. “We’ll replace Google Search, we’ll build our own smartphones, we’ll build better infra. We’ll remove all the ads and de-enshittify the entire tech world.”
“Software is over,” he gloated in an earlier comment, claiming to have “one-shotted Photoshop. The whole thing.”
Kyle Orland has been the Senior Gaming Editor at Ars Technica since 2012, writing primarily about the business, tech, and culture behind video games. He has journalism and computer science degrees from University of Maryland. He once wrote a whole book about Minesweeper.
Can anyone explain to me how this process isn't software piracy?
The idea of a clean room implementation relies on multiple human actors. One team writing specs and another totally different team reading them.
This is one team running a tool against a binary, then running that same tool against the product of the first run. That not even remotely close to a clean room implementation.
The problem is that we're not really set up legally to handle this. Creating software used to require a fair amount of skill just to get something which worked and most people with that skill weren't just going to do the incredibly tedious work of taking someone else's program, mapping out exactly how every bit of it worked, and writing their own code to do exactly the same thing. Copying was either copying source (which copyright law clearly covers) or at the level of ideas and concepts which copyright doesn't really cover: in Apple v. Microsoft and HP in the 90s, it was an established fact that Microsoft Windows added features which Mac OS had years before but Apple lost all but one of the claims because the court didn't agree that Apple could claim the broader GUI concepts as opposed to very narrow implementations (the one claim they got was that HP's trash can looked too much like the Mac's, which is one reason why Windows uses a recycling bin).
So that left most of the industry with two common paths: bottom feeders would copy code illegally but were relatively easily caught as well because the code was so similar (e.g. in the QuickTime / Video for Windows suit, it was exactly the same code used by an unethical contractor and Microsoft quickly removed it because it was completely unambiguously not their code) or there's a broad conceptual inspiration but the underlying code is relatively different except where there are domain similarities (e.g. a JPEG decoder will have a lot of terms with the same names due to implementing the same spec and the underlying math has to be the same). This wasn't perfect but it kept the problem at a manageable level because the people with the skills to clone things usually could do more valuable things and larger businesses knew they'd get caught (back when the DOJ enforced laws) so you had some problems like the guys who'd download games from the Play/App Store, repackage them, and change enough of the visible assets not to be caught, but those were small scale operations because it's straightforward to analyze compiled binaries and show the underlying structure is highly similar. There wasn't enough money to be made in the confusion / knock-off market to support hiring more / better-skilled people to do a better job cloning big apps or keeping up with new developments.
AI changes that because you can task an LLM with all of the tedious work of mapping out how the original app works, generating code to mimic that behavior, and while it's still going to require a fair amount of work to correctly implement functionality and correct confabulations, it's still a lot more feasible for a one person project than it would have been 5 years ago. LLMs also tirelessly repeat that process with each release so the upstream can't rely on moving faster than a single knock-off artist can keep up.
Again, none of this is perfect and getting anywhere near the same level of quality (even for Adobe/Microsoft levels) is going to take time but it's reducing the number of people needed considerably and especially reducing the skill level. For example, the number of people who could create a game's code, artwork, and sound on their own is a relatively small group compared to the number of people who could, say, have a coding agent handle a lot of the code and an image/audio generator fill in the gaps instead of hiring artists and voice actors, and the lower end mobile / Steam market makes it hard for small players to stand out in search results compared to the number of people who are going to search for Photoshop but use anything else (i.e. their class / boss gives them a copy).
I think this is going to hurt smaller indie developers first because they don't have the massive name recognition and legal departments which Adobe or Microsoft have and the resource levels are more comparable: the small indie team has to spend a lot of time developing the concept & behavior for an app so if they have, say, a 5-10 person company they're not as well positioned to stay ahead of a small 1-2 person clone shop which doesn't have to do the hard R&D.

pages.title: [AI Breaking News] All Adobe products made free via AI clones, the era where Claude handles operations begins｜ノクト
pages.text:
[AI Breaking News] All Adobe products made free via AI clones, the era where Claude handles operations begins
*This article contains affiliate links (PR).
Using Claude and Opus 5.5, someone has released seven major Adobe software programs entirely for free as open source. However, after reading about it, I thought, 'This isn't just a story about making things free; it's the gateway to an era where AI agents directly operate software.' It's not just the superficial fact that you can get a Photoshop alternative for free; I felt the real point is the 'mechanism by which AI masters tools' behind it. I will organize this in order.
Seven major Adobe products have been re-implemented from scratch by AI and released for free
These are designed to be directly operated by AI agents (such as Claude)
Even as generative AI becomes omnipotent, a 'place to manually refine details' is still needed
🎯 7 answers you will get from this article
✅ What did the group ArtCraft do?
✅ Why is clean-room re-implementation legally important?
✅ How usable are PhotoCraft and FilmCraft really?
✅ Why can Claude operate these software programs?
✅ What is the role of the agents.md file?
✅ Why are these tools still necessary even now that video generation AI has evolved?
✅ What can business professionals try starting tomorrow?
Chapter 1: Summary of the video's claims — What was discussed
Chapter 2: Interpretation from my own industry experience
Chapter 3: Perspectives not covered in the video
Chapter 5: Conclusion | 5 ironclad rules from this article
Chapter 1: Summary of the video's claims — What was discussed
The core of this video is that a group called ArtCraft used Claude's Opus 5.5 to rebuild the Adobe product suite from scratch and release it for free.
Seven pieces of software were released. The Photoshop alternative is "PhotoCraft", the Premiere alternative is "FilmCraft," and the After Effects alternative is "EffectCraft." Furthermore, they have "VectorCraft" as an Illustrator alternative, "DesignCraft" as an InDesign alternative, "LightCraft" as a Lightroom alternative, and even "PDFCraft" as an Acrobat alternative.
The implementation language is Rust, and it is explained that they were "clean-room reimplemented" using Opus 5.5. In other words, the claim is that they did not disassemble or analyze (reverse engineer) existing Adobe software, but rather rewrote it from scratch by looking only at the functional specifications. This is cited as the basis for why it is legally clear.
The release location is getartcraft.com/apps, and the code can also be obtained from GitHub (github.com/storytold). PhotoCraft reportedly gained 20,000 stars just a few hours after its release. In the video, demos of actually operating PhotoCraft and FilmCraft were shown, introducing how many elements that people who usually use Adobe products would find "familiar," such as layer styles, timeline zoom functions, and shortcut keys, have been reproduced.
What is important here is the point that this does not end as just a "free clone festival." In the latter half of the video, there is a discussion about how these software programs are designed on the premise that they will be operated directly by AI agents, especially Claude.
Specifically, a CLI (command-line interface) is built into each piece of software, and a Markdown file called "agents.md" is provided. This is like an operation handbook for agents, and by having agents like Claude read this, they can understand the functions and operation methods of each software and proceed with tasks autonomously.
In the video, a demo was actually shown where an entire animation with layers was generated just by throwing a single prompt at EffectCraft (the After Effects alternative). It also showed how a magazine spread layout is created by Claude in DesignCraft (the InDesign alternative).
The conclusion that can be drawn: The core of this video is that this release is not just about "free Adobe," but is designed as an experimental ground for AI agents to directly operate creative software.
Chapter 2: Interpretation from my own industry experience
2-1. How this hits home in current practical work
Many people use image editing and video editing software in marketing and side-hustle settings, but honestly, Adobe's subscription costs are not a small burden. Even Photoshop alone costs several thousand yen per month, and the Creative Cloud complete plan is even higher. For sole proprietors and freelancers, this fixed cost hits surprisingly hard, like a body blow.
What this ArtCraft release shows is the possibility that the "value of the tool itself" is starting to decline relatively. As mentioned in the video, much of what can be done in Photoshop was reproduced with considerable accuracy in just a few weeks of development and a few days of release. Of course, there is a disclaimer that it is not a perfect replica, but it cannot be overlooked that it is at a level that can cover the majority of daily editing tasks.
However, what we should be calm about here is that a simple judgment of "switching because it's free" is premature. If you are using it for business, you need to judge it including factors such as compatibility, support systems, and integration with existing files. I think it is appropriate to view this as a stage where "options have increased."
Although not mentioned in the video, I felt that this could become a kind of "insurance" for people who take on video editing as a side hustle.
For example, situations where your Premiere license suddenly expires during client work, or the timing for paying high renewal fees doesn't align, are common in practice. In such cases, an open-source version like FilmCraft could function as a "temporary substitute." Of course, it is high-risk to suddenly use it for production in a professional setting, but there should be plenty of room to consider it for rough cuts or testing purposes.
Also, the fact that it supports agent operations is an interesting implication from a practical standpoint. Software that comes standard with an "AI operation manual" like agents.md is a sign that "ease of integration with AI" will become one of the evaluation criteria for selecting business tools in the future. This may be an element that will also be required for Adobe products themselves.
Conclusion: Beyond being free, the realization from a practical perspective is that "whether it is designed to be easily handled by AI" is becoming a new standard for choosing tools.
Chapter 3: Perspectives not covered in the video
3-1. Counterarguments and alternative cases
The video explained that it is "legal because it is a clean-room re-implementation," but this was merely introduced as the creator's claim. The video did not touch upon how Adobe would actually react or how the similarity in trademarks and the appearance of features would be judged.
Since the video mentioned the name PhotoCraft and the high degree of reproduction of layer styles, the boundary between "imitation of functionality" and "imitation of appearance/experience" may become a topic of debate in the future. The video remained optimistic about this point throughout, but I think it is healthy for the reader to understand that "this is an issue that has not yet been settled."
Another point often overlooked is the instability behind the speed of being released within hours to days. The video also included the statement, "Of course, it's not a perfect replica, after all, it was released 24 hours ago." In other words, one must not forget the premise that this is software that has not yet matured (is not stable).
The expectation that improvements will proceed in an open-source and community-driven manner was also discussed in the video, but that also means "there is no support system at this time." The video did not emphasize that if you adopt it for full-scale business use, bug handling and preparation for data loss risks are your own responsibility.
Conclusion: I think the way to read it without being swept away by the enthusiasm of the video is to evaluate it with the premise that both legality and quality are "still in development at this time."
4-1. Concrete actions you can take starting tomorrow
Access getartcraft.com/apps, and first download one software you are interested in (such as PhotoCraft or FilmCraft) for free and try it out.
Instead of using production data, check "how much it reproduces" in your usual workflow using light test materials.
Confirm the existence of agents.md and try instructing an agent like Claude to perform simple editing tasks (text changes, layer adjustments, etc.).
The idea discussed in the video of "AI for the first draft, manual work for the finishing touches" can be applied directly to practical work. For example, for SNS banner images or simple logo animations, it is suitable to send a prompt to Claude and have it create a rough first draft on EffectCraft or PhotoCraft. The video also pointed out that "if it's a logo animation, it can be made sufficiently with a video generation model," but it was stated that for long-form editing work that requires layer management, it is more efficient to have Claude create the first draft with these tools.
On the other hand, for final deliverables for clients or work where you want to be particular about the details of color and placement, the conclusion of the video is that the process of humans moving their hands to make fine adjustments cannot be omitted. From the statement that "fine adjustments are much easier if you are well-versed in the tool," I feel that the realistic compromise is a division of labor where humans polish the first draft created by AI, rather than leaving everything to AI.
Conclusion: If you assume a division of roles where "AI does the first draft and humans do the finishing touches," there is plenty of room to incorporate even free tools into practical work.
Chapter 5: Summary | 5 Iron Rules of This Article
ArtCraft has re-implemented 7 Adobe products from scratch using Claude (Opus 5.5) and Rust, and released them for free
The claim of 'clean room re-implementation' is the basis for its legality, but it has not yet been verified by third parties
The biggest feature is its design, which allows AI agents to operate it directly, such as via agents.md or CLI
Keep in mind that this is software released just now, and its stability and support system are still in development
A division of labor style of 'AI for the first draft, humans for the finishing touches' is the realistic way to use it at this moment

pages.title: Salesforce (CRM) Is ‘Sticky’ In The AI Era, Jim Cramer Said & Remarked That Amateurs Can Beat Adobe
pages.text:

Salesforce (CRM) Is ‘Sticky’ In The AI Era, Jim Cramer Said & Remarked That Amateurs Can Beat Adobe
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 1:55 PM CDT 5 min read
Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) and Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE) are two stocks that Jim Cramer frequently discusses. For both, most of his remarks are about AI and the role that the firms are playing in the sector. The CNBC TV host has frequently defended Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and his artificial intelligence initiatives and discussed the impact of AI on Adobe. In his morning appearance on the 12th, Cramer continued to comment on Adobe's business model and whether it could withstand the competitive pressures in the age of easy software development fueled by artificial intelligence:
"Now also. We also have a double downgrade of Adobe. That's Wells Fargo, Salesforce was Bank of America. What I think what's most interesting, Adobe is easier to copy and I think people have been doing it. You and I discussed that in the break. Adobe's very expensive. People feel that perhaps it is no longer worth this much. Because of Claude. Because of ChatGPT. . .the 660 dollar. Now this is very interesting David. Salesforce had a fantastic Dreamforce and a great quarter. And people are kind of coming around to think that maybe there's no disintermediation, that it's really Monday.com, smaller outfits, Hubspot. What's interesting is that the guy did wait, the analyst did wait till it came back. So it wasn't like a, well I bought it at the top situation. A lot of it has to do with what's sticky. And what's not. And Salesforce is regarded as very sticky, it gets in the organization, people like it when they use it. And Adobe is regarded as being easy to disrupt, whether it be from Canva, whether it be from Figma, whether it be from, the, I don't know, I subscribe to Adobe and I just find that, you can kind of fool around with it on an amateur basis and beat it."
Cramer's faith in Salesforce has been rewarding. The shares are up by 20% since late August after closing 22% higher on August 27th. Ahead of the gain, the CNBC TV host discussed Salesforce in detail, which we covered as part of Jim Cramer Discussed These 22 Stocks Including A Hidden Oil & Energy Play.
Jim Cramer Sees a Telling Change in Broadcom’s (AVGO) Stock
For Salesforce, Cramer built on the earlier comments we've linked above. He extended his take to outline that Salesforce was sticky with businesses and was making durable inroads into businesses. The remarks are central to the firm's hypothesis as for Salesforce, the debate has centered around the durability and popularity of its AI initiatives.
On this front, the firm's second quarter earnings saw its Agentforce platform's annual recurring revenue grow by a massive 240% annually to touch $1.5 billion. The Agentforce growth validates what Cramer's been 'hearing' as it indicates that the AI platform is making inroads into the business world. As for the 'stickiness', current remaining performance obligations (cRPO), which measures revenue from signed and contracted customer agreements for the next 12 months, grew by 14% annually to touch $33.5 billion. Zooming specifically on AI, during the earnings call, chief revenue officer Miguel Milano outlined that "Customers that start the agentic journey with Salesforce, on average, they are already at double the AOV with a perspective of nearly quadrupling, 3x-4x the AOV." AOV is annual order value and Milano's comments indicate that AI is making a real impact on the income statement.
Judging by these metrics, you'd be surprised to know that Salesforce didn't make it on our list of the 10 Most Promising Technology Stocks to Buy Right Now. The top stock on the list does have billions of dollars in debt.
Speaking of debt, the quarter also saw Salesforce's noncurrent debt jumped by a whopping 276% to sit at $39.3 billion. The jump was due to financing activities related to share buybacks and the like. Additionally, while earnings per share jumped by 103% to $5.90, $2.53 of the EPS came from investment gains. This indicated that perhaps the AI gains were yet to translate to the bottom line - a fact bolstered by Agentforce ARR being a small portion of Salesforce's overall revenue of $11.35 billion.
Looking at Adobe, its subscription business has not only been on Jim Cramer's radar but also in his crosshairs for months now. For instance, in February, Cramer remarked that "Apple put out a very competitive product to Firefly the other day, I think. I may have to cancel my subscription." For more, check out 15 Stocks on Jim Cramer's Radar.
While Cramer believes that Adobe is easy to substitute, the firm's fiscal third quarter saw its monthly active users cross the one billion mark while its annual recurring revenue and remaining performance obligations grew by 11.2% and 8% annually. For Adobe, a major victim of the AI wave, the fact that management also outlined that AI-first ARR grew by 150% indicated that the firm might be improving reslience against the emerging technology.
Looking at the valuation, Salesforce, through its forward P/E ratio of 27.78 is more richly valued than Adobe, which trades at 8.73. With Adobe's historic range being 25x and 45x, the market appears to be pricing in an extreme disruption. Additionally, while the ratio implies a yield of 11.45%, this could very well be a value trap. For Salesforce, it suggests that the market is quite optimistic. The hedge funds are siding with the market, as 99 had disclosed a stake in Salesforce in Q2 compared to 81 for Adobe, according to Insider Monkey's data.

Adobe is Being Punished for a Creative Cannibalization Threat That Isn’t Real
Adobe's stock has cratered 32% this year even as its AI revenue grows triple digits, leaving investors caught between a compelling valuation and a nagging question about whether the real threat to Creative Cloud has barely started.
Published October 13, 2026, 8:45am ET · 3 min read
Adobe is a multinational software company best known for its Photoshop and Acrobat. © Adobe logo (CC by 2.0) by midiman
Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE | ADBE Price Prediction) trades at $238.14. The market is pricing in a generative AI disruption that the company’s own results keep failing to show.
Adobe owns the professional creative stack (Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere) along with Acrobat and a large enterprise marketing business. Shares are down 31.96% year to date, even though the company just posted its fifth consecutive EPS beat. The pressure got worse after Barron’s reported a downgrade to Sell, citing growth concerns and “meaningful cracks now starting to show.”
AI Revenue Is Surging While the Multiple Collapses
Bulls point to the AI numbers. AI-first ending ARR now tops $650 million and is growing more than 150% year over year. Firefly ARR grew 40% quarter over quarter, and creative freemium users passed 100 million. Management also said AI credit consumption is accelerating inside the core desktop apps. Creators are using generative AI through Adobe’s tools.
The stock trades at a forward P/E of 9 with a PEG of 0.582, which is a deep-value multiple for a business that just raised full-year non-GAAP EPS guidance to $24.45 to $24.50. Adobe also bought back about 9.5 million shares for $2.232 billion in a single quarter.
Slowing down ARR and Thinner Margins Feed the Sell Calls
Bears focus on what lies behind the beats. In the latest quarter, net income rose only 3.1% on revenue growth of 12.89%. Full-year ending ARR growth is targeted at just 10.2%. On the call, analysts pressed management about lower net new ARR and seat-volume weakness. Management had also put off price increases, choosing to push users into the freemium model first.
Canva, Midjourney and OpenAI keep competing for lighter creative work. Retail sentiment is negative too: a Reddit post called “ADOBE is cooked.” drew 1,509 upvotes.
A CEO Handoff Leaves the Story Half Written
Shantanu Narayen is leaving after 18 years as CEO, and Anil Chakravarthy is taking over. The freemium strategy has not yet shown that it converts users into paying customers at scale. Upcoming markers include Q4 revenue against guidance of $6.8 to $6.85 billion, the first ARR outlook under the new CEO, and evidence that freemium users are turning into ARR.
Wall Street Sees Upside but Mostly Rates It Hold
At $238.14, Adobe lies 15.5% below the consensus target of $275.06 from 39 analysts. Price targets are one data point and come with no guarantee. The ratings break down this way:
Over the past year, Adobe fell 29.44% while the S&P 500 gained 19.15%. The trailing P/E is 14.
Adobe’s Results Keep Defying the Cannibalization Thesis
At $238.14, the data points to a business the market may be mispricing.
Part of the threat is real. Net new ARR is slowing down, and low-end tools are winning casual users. The bigger claim, that AI will replace Creative Cloud, is still unproven. Creative and marketing subscription revenue grew 13% year over year, and AI usage is rising inside Adobe’s main apps.
The likely path higher runs through a seasonally strong enterprise Q4, product launches at Adobe MAX, and the Topaz Labs deal. At a single-digit forward multiple, much of the bad news already looks priced in. This outlook falls apart if AI-first ARR stalls or creative subscription growth slips toward single digits.
Adobe is being valued like a business AI is replacing, even as its AI revenue grows faster than almost anything else it sells.

pages.title: CORRECTING and REPLACING Adobe: U.S. Holiday Shopping Season to Hit Record $275.1 Billion Online, Rising 6.7% YoY
pages.text:
Skip to navigation Skip to main content Skip to right column
This is a paid press release. Contact the press release distributor directly with any inquiries.
CORRECTING and REPLACING Adobe: U.S. Holiday Shopping Season to Hit Record $275.1 Billion Online, Rising 6.7% YoY
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 11:56 AM CDT 8 min read
Cyber Monday set to remain the biggest online shopping day of the season—with consumers spending over $15 billion in a single day—but Black Friday will see stronger growth due to earlier discounts.
Consumers are expected to take advantage of competitive deals this season (up to 30% off listed price) to stock up on essentials such as personal hygiene and household cleaning products.
The overall shopping journey continues to evolve, as consumers embrace AI tools and social influencers to find deals and learn about specific products, while continuing to leverage Buy Now Pay Later when they are ready to transact.
SAN JOSE, Calif., October 16, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--First parenthetical note in the "Pre-season shopping in October continues to accelerate" section of release dated Sept. 28, 2026 should read "which became an annual tradition in 2022" (instead of "which began in 2021").
The updated release reads:
ADOBE: U.S. HOLIDAY SHOPPING SEASON TO HIT RECORD $275.1 BILLION ONLINE, RISING 6.7% YOY
Cyber Monday set to remain the biggest online shopping day of the season—with consumers spending over $15 billion in a single day—but Black Friday will see stronger growth due to earlier discounts.
Consumers are expected to take advantage of competitive deals this season (up to 30% off listed price) to stock up on essentials such as personal hygiene and household cleaning products.
The overall shopping journey continues to evolve, as consumers embrace AI tools and social influencers to find deals and learn about specific products, while continuing to leverage Buy Now Pay Later when they are ready to transact.
Adobe (Nasdaq: ADBE) released today its online shopping forecast for the 2026 holiday season, covering the period from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, 2026. Based on Adobe Analytics data, the analysis provides the most comprehensive view into U.S. e-commerce by analyzing direct transactions online. Adobe's forecast is based on over 1 trillion visits to U.S. retail sites, 100 million SKUs and 18 product categories—more than any other technology company or research organization. Adobe Analytics is part of Adobe CX Enterprise, relied upon by global brands to accelerate Customer Experience Orchestration, connecting data, content and AI to deliver real-time, personalized interactions.
2026 holidays set to cross $275 billion milestone, with pre-season spending uptick in October
Adobe expects U.S. online sales to hit $275.1 billion this holiday season (Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, 2026), growing 6.7% year-over-year (YoY). Cyber Week (the five-day period between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday) is set to drive $47.5 billion online (up 7.4% YoY), representing 17.3% of the full holiday season spend.
Cyber Monday (Nov. 30) is expected to set a new milestone for U.S. e-commerce, with consumers spending over $15 billion online in a single day ($15.1 billion, up 6.2% YoY). The second biggest day of the season will be Black Friday ($12.9 billion, up 9.2% YoY), which is growing faster than Cyber Monday—driven in part by having the biggest discounts for categories such as TVs, apparel and appliances. Thanksgiving is set to drive $6.9 billion (up 8.5% YoY), bolstered by impulse shopping: A record 63% of online spend is set to come through mobile devices (up from 61.6% in 2025), outpacing the full season where mobile will account for 57.4% of overall spend (up from 56.4% in 2025).
Of the full holiday season spend, electronics ($63.3 billion, up 5.9% YoY) and apparel ($51.3 billion, up 4.7% YoY) remain tentpole categories in e-commerce, but consumers are also embracing other categories online with stronger growth observed in furniture ($33.4 billion, up 7.3% YoY), grocery ($26.1 billion, up 10.3% YoY), toys ($9.6 billion, up 9.6% YoY) and cosmetics ($9.2 billion, 9.5% YoY).
Pre-season shopping in October continues to accelerate
The Prime Day event in October (which became an annual tradition in 2022) has become an industrywide e-commerce moment, with discounts happening broadly across U.S. retailers. It is now driving significant consumer spend in advance of the holiday season. Adobe expects $95.8 billion will be spent online in October 2026, up a notable 8% YoY. Nearly $10 billion will be spent during the Prime Day event from October 6 to 7 ($9.9 billion, up 9.2% YoY), driven in part by discounts that are set to peak at 19% off listed price. This has changed the shape of the holiday season, pushing U.S. retailers to manage promotions and inventory effectively to capture an additional pre-season spike in shopping interest.
Consumers expected to take advantage of strong discounts to stock up on essentials
Adobe expects competitive discounts this holiday season, up to 30% off listed price (during Cyber Week). Shoppers will see deals throughout the season, up to 14% in early November, up to 21% just before Thanksgiving and up to 10-15% throughout December.
Across categories, deals will be on par with the 2025 season: Discounts in electronics for example, are expected to peak at 30% off listed price (vs. 30.1% in 2025), while discounts for toys are set to hit 29% (vs. 28%). Notable discounts are also expected in TVs at 23% (vs. 24.2%), computers at 23% (vs. 22.8%), apparel at 23% (vs. 23.2%), sporting goods at 19% (vs. 19.5%), appliances at 18% (vs. 19.2%) and furniture at 18% (vs. 19%). Shoppers will find the deepest discounts for electronics and computers on Cyber Monday, but the best deals for TVs, toys, apparel, appliances and furniture is expected to land on Black Friday. Thanksgiving will have the best deals for sporting goods.
While consumers have historically embraced holiday deals to buy gifts or adopt the latest gadgets, many are taking advantage of discounts to stock up on essentials. During Cyber Week, online sales of personal hygiene products are expected to jump 150% (compared to average sales levels in September 2026) and clothing basics by 210%. Other essentials set to see a boost include baby products (up 113%), pet products (up 93%) and household cleaning items (up 49%).
Buy Now Pay Later to drive over $21 billion in holiday season spend
The flexible payment method continues to see traction amongst consumers during the holiday season. Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) is expected to drive $21.3 billion (Nov-Dec), up 6.6% YoY. Usage is set to spike on Cyber Monday, where BNPL will be used for $1.09 billion in online spend. This is the second consecutive year where over a billion dollars were driven by BNPL on Cyber Monday. On Black Friday, BNPL is set to drive $807 million in online spend. Most of BNPL spend will come through mobile devices (82% share vs. desktop), showing the impact of impulse shopping on driving adoption of the payment method.
Another AI-powered holiday season: In the 2024 holiday season, Adobe observed the first uptick in consumers using AI-powered chat and browser services for online shopping (from finding deals to quickly locating products). Adobe expects AI traffic to U.S. retail sites this holiday season (measured by shoppers clicking on a link) to rise 130% YoY. The biggest uptick is expected on Thanksgiving (up 159% YoY), followed by Black Friday (up 95% YoY) and Cyber Monday (up 88% YoY). In an Adobe survey* of 5,000 consumers, 77% of respondents who have used AI for online shopping report feeling more confident in their purchase, and 69% say they are less likely to return an item they bought.
Hot sellers: Top gaming consoles this season are expected to include Nintendo Switch 2, Sony PlayStation 5/Pro and Xbox Series X, along with games such as Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, EA SPORTS FC 27, Grand Theft Auto VI, Madden NFL 27, Marvel's Wolverine, Minecraft Dungeons II, NBA 2K27 and Pokémon Pokopia. Top selling toys are expected to include Beyblade X, Jellycat plush toys, KPop Demon Hunters toys, LEGO Pokémon and SMART Play, NeeDoh Toys, Pokémon Pikachu Puppetronic, Sesame Street Tickle Me Elmo Giggle Max and Toy Story 5 toys. Other expected hot sellers include AirPods Pro 3​, Dyson Airwrap​, Google Pixel 11​, iPhone 18 Pro​, iPhone Duo, KODAK Charmera​, Meta AI Glasses, Oura Ring 5​, Samsung Galaxy S26/Z Fold8​ and WHOOP 5.0.
Social media and affiliates drive purchase behavior: Adobe measures the impact of different marketing investments during the holiday season, looking at its contribution to revenue. Affiliates/partners (which includes social influencers) and social media overall are set to see the biggest gains in share of revenue, up 12% and 17%, respectively. In comparison, paid search is expected to rise by 4%. Within the affiliates/partner category, cashback and rewards partners leads in affiliate traffic with a 36% share, followed by influencers and creators at 22%. For U.S. retailers, this highlights the importance of partner and social-led acquisition during the holiday season.

Adobe, HubSpot, Workday, Asana, and Workiva Shares Are Soaring, What You Need To Know
What Happened?
A number of stocks jumped in the afternoon session after software-as-a-service and broader technology equities rebounded as falling Treasury yields attracted dip-buyers back into the market following a sharp, AI-driven sell-off in previous sessions.
As reported by CNBC, major equity averages—including the tech-heavy Nasdaq—moved higher as market sentiment stabilized and capital rotated back into quality software. In the previous session, CNBC noted that shares across the artificial intelligence and broader technology space had faced heightened selling pressure, rattling investor confidence regarding near-term monetization and the heavy debt burdens funding the AI sector.
However, CNBC observed that this pullback proved short-lived as dip-buyers re-entered the market, viewing the sector's valuation reset as an attractive entry point for companies with fortress balance sheets. Contributing heavily to the improved sentiment, CNBC reported that the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield—which recently hit its highest point since 2002—pulled back, providing a crucial reprieve for the market. CNBC highlighted this relationship, explaining that falling yields provide a tailwind for high-growth SaaS stocks because lower interest rates make the long-dated future cash flows of these tech companies more attractive to investors.
Ultimately, CNBC noted that this swift recovery highlights an enduring investor appetite for leading software firms, even as Wall Street remains highly sensitive to how quickly massive capital investments in artificial intelligence will translate into sustainable corporate profits.

Adobe and NVIDIA Expand Collaboration to Speed Agentic Creation
Thu, October 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM CDT 7 min read
Adobe is expanding its collaboration with NVIDIA to optimize its flagship tools including Adobe Photoshop, Premiere, Substance 3D, Frame.io and Brand Concierge, delivering faster AI-powered creation, production and personalization.
Adobe is bringing the power of the NVIDIA RTX Spark superchip to its agentic creative applications Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D. Optimized to take full advantage of RTX Spark, these applications deliver up to 2x faster AI processing, editing, color and effects, helping creatives iterate faster and stay in their creative flow.
Adobe Brand Concierge is now optimized with NVIDIA Nemotron open models, providing enterprises a flexible and efficient way to deliver high-quality conversational experiences at scale, with NVIDIA also selecting Brand Concierge to power relevant and contextual customer interactions on NVIDIA.com.
SAN JOSE, Calif., October 15, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Adobe (Nasdaq: ADBE), the global technology leader that unleashes creativity, productivity and customer experiences through innovative tools and platforms, and NVIDIA today announced an expansion of their partnership to optimize Adobe's flagship tools including Adobe Photoshop, Premiere, Substance 3D, Frame.io and Brand Concierge, delivering faster AI-powered creation, production and personalization.
This work builds on Adobe and NVIDIA's strategic partnership announced in March, which brings together Adobe's creative and marketing workflows, models and technology with NVIDIA's open models, libraries, research and accelerated computing to accelerate creative, production and marketing workflows across video, images, 3D and other creative media. That collaboration includes GPU acceleration for media ingestion and intelligence in Frame.io, as well as ongoing work around Adobe Substance 3D, Adobe Firefly Foundry and 3D digital twin workflows for enterprise customers.
"Creative workflows are more multimodal than ever, with many projects spanning images, video, audio, motion and 3D, making performance critical to helping creatives stay focused on their ideas and craft," said Deepa Subramaniam, vice president, product marketing, creative professionals, Adobe. "By partnering with NVIDIA to optimize Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D for RTX Spark and accelerating Frame.io in the cloud, we're delivering the performance creatives need to bring their ideas to life."
"AI agents are helping creators unlock deeper and richer workflows using the Adobe applications they know and love," said Jason Paul, vice president, local AI, NVIDIA. "Powered by RTX Spark, Adobe's optimized tools deliver up to 2x faster performance to accelerate these new workflows."
Empowering Creatives With Faster Adobe Tools Rearchitected With NVIDIA
Creative professionals today move between image, video, motion and 3D, sometimes all within the same project. As AI increasingly becomes part of the creative process, they need technology that keeps pace with the speed of their ideas and the complexity of their workflows. As an industry leader in creativity, Adobe's tools apply decades of creative expertise to amplify human potential and make it easier to quickly turn ideas into impactful work.
Adobe is bringing the power of the NVIDIA RTX Spark superchip, which NVIDIA launched earlier this month, to its agentic creative applications Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D. RTX-accelerated and optimized to take full advantage of RTX Spark's unified memory and AI compute, these applications deliver up to 2x faster AI processing, editing, color and effects, helping creatives iterate faster and stay in their creative flow.
Adobe rearchitected Photoshop around GPU-accelerated compositing to be faster and more responsive for creative tasks from removing distractions with the Remove Tool to applying effects like Gaussian Blur and Light Leaks directly on canvas.
Some of the most demanding post-production workflows in Premiere, from playback and rendering, to effects, color and AI-powered tools, are RTX-accelerated and optimized for RTX Spark. This results in real, tangible speed gains for popular audio and video features in Premiere like Enhance Speech and Object Mask. For 3D artists using Substance 3D Painter, RTX Spark speeds up the heaviest steps around texturing.
Accelerating Cloud Video Workflows With Frame.io and NVIDIA
Adobe is also using NVIDIA accelerated computing to speed cloud media processing and intelligent content discovery for Adobe Frame.io, helping production teams find and use growing media libraries faster. The updated Frame.io pipeline uses NVIDIA video acceleration, including NVIDIA NVDEC for hardware-accelerated decoding and NVIDIA TensorRT ™ with CUDA™ for content preprocessing and embedding generation.
Moving compute-intensive video decoding, preprocessing and embedding generation onto NVIDIA GPUs lets Frame.io process media faster and make it searchable sooner, while supporting more responsive discovery across large content libraries.
Early performance results from selected Frame.io transcode and search workloads show:
Approximately 5x faster embedding generation
4-5x improvement in P95 processing latency
An approximately 80% smaller search proxy
For creative teams, these gains mean uploaded content becomes searchable sooner, larger libraries refresh more efficiently, and discovery and review stay frictionless as media volumes grow.
Personalized Conversational Experiences With Adobe Brand Concierge Optimized On NVIDIA Nemotron
Brands also want more choice and value from the AI models powering personalized experiences. Open models can help meet that need, providing a flexible and efficient way to deliver high-quality, responsive conversations at enterprise scale.
Adobe and NVIDIA worked together to optimize Brand Concierge using NVIDIA Nemotron™ open models. This version will be available to enterprise customers later this year. NVIDIA has also selected Brand Concierge to drive personalized conversational experiences grounded in organizational data and content. This enables NVIDIA to tailor interactions on their website based on customer needs, while leveraging Nemotron to deliver fast, high-quality responses at scale.
Get ready for what's next — with three days of creative skill-building, visionary keynotes and valuable connections at Adobe MAX, running Nov. 10-12. Adobe and NVIDIA will showcase the latest advancements for creators alongside their hardware partners.
Adobe (Nasdaq: ADBE) empowers everyone to create through industry-leading platforms and tools that unleash creativity, productivity and personalized customer experiences. For more information, visit www.adobe.com.
